content: Pyridine is a chemical compound with the molecular formula C5H5N. It is a liquid characterized by a distinctively unpleasant, fish-like odor. Structurally, pyridine is a simple and fundamentally important heterocyclic aromatic organic compound. It is closely related to benzene, with one CH group in the six-membered ring replaced by a nitrogen atom. The pyridine ring is a structural component in many biologically and chemically significant compounds, including nicotinamides. Pyridine is also utilized as a ligand in coordination chemistry, where it is commonly abbreviated as py. Pyridine exhibits basicity due to the lone pair of electrons on its nitrogen atom. This lone pair is not delocalized into the aromatic π-system, which makes pyridine chemically similar to tertiary amines. When pyridine reacts with acids, it becomes protonated, forming a positively charged aromatic polyatomic ion known as the pyridinium cation. The bond lengths and angles in pyridine and its protonated form, the pyridinium ion, remain nearly identical because protonation does not disrupt the aromatic π-system. Pyridine is widely employed as a versatile solvent due to its polar but aprotic nature. It is fully miscible with a broad range of solvents, including both hexane and water. Deuterated pyridine, known as pyridine-d5, is frequently used as a solvent in proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. In industrial organic chemistry, pyridine plays a critical role as both a fundamental building block and a solvent or reagent in organic synthesis. It is used as a solvent in Knoevenagel condensations and as a mild reducing agent with improved stability in protic solvents compared to sodium borohydride (NaBH4). Pyridine-sulfur trioxide (C5H5NSO3) is a sulfonation agent employed to convert alcohols into sulfonates, which can subsequently undergo C-O bond cleavage upon reduction with hydride agents. Pyridine is also a precursor in the synthesis of compounds used as intermediates in the production of insecticides, herbicides, pharmaceuticals, food flavorings, dyes, rubber chemicals, adhesives, paints, explosives, and disinfectants. Additionally, it serves as a denaturant for antifreeze mixtures, ethyl alcohol, and fungicides, and as a dyeing aid in the textile industry. Pyridine can be synthesized through various methods in both industrial and laboratory settings. Industrially, it is obtained from crude coal tar or synthesized from acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, and ammonia. The Hantzsch pyridine synthesis is a multicomponent reaction involving formaldehyde, a keto-ester, and a nitrogen donor. Other methods include the reaction of 1,5-diketones with ammonium acetate in acetic acid followed by oxidation (the Kröhnke pyridine synthesis), the Zincke reaction to produce pyridinium salts, and the Ciamician-Dennstedt rearrangement, which expands the pyrrole ring with dichlorocarbene to form 3-chloropyridine. The Chichibabin pyridine synthesis involves three equivalents of a linear aldehyde and ammonia. In organic reactions, pyridine behaves both as a tertiary amine and as an aromatic compound. It undergoes protonation, alkylation, acylation, and N-oxidation at the nitrogen atom. Pyridine is also susceptible to nucleophilic aromatic substitution at the C2 and C4 positions, as seen in the Chichibabin reaction, where pyridine reacts with sodium amide to form 2-aminopyridine. In the Emmert reaction, pyridine reacts with a ketone in the presence of aluminum or magnesium and mercuric chloride to yield a carbinol derivative at the C2 position. Pyridine is toxic, with an oral LD50 of 891 mg/kg in rats. It is volatile and can be absorbed through the skin. Studies indicate that exposure to pyridine in drinking water reduces sperm motility in mice at all dose levels and increases estrous cycle length in rats at the highest dose level. Current evaluations of pyridine's carcinogenic potential suggest inadequate evidence in humans, though limited evidence exists for carcinogenic effects in animals. Acute pyridine intoxication can cause dizziness, headache, nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, and pulmonary congestion. Despite its resistance to oxidation, pyridine is readily degraded by bacteria, releasing ammonium and carbon dioxide as terminal degradation products. Structurally or chemically related compounds include: 4-Dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), a derivative of pyridine. Bipyridine and viologen, which are simple polypyridine compounds consisting of two pyridine molecules joined by a single bond. Terpyridine, a molecule composed of three pyridine rings connected by two single bonds. Quinoline and isoquinoline, which are fused-ring systems containing both a pyridine and a benzene ring. Aniline, a benzene derivative with an attached NH2 group, which is not a pyridine derivative. Diazines, such as pyrazine and pyrimidine, which have one additional carbon replaced by nitrogen. Triazines, with two additional carbons replaced by nitrogen, and tetrazines, with four nitrogen atoms. 2,6-Lutidine, a trivial name for 2,6-dimethylpyridine. Collidine, the trivial name for 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine. Pyridinium p-toluenesulfonate (PPTS), a salt formed by proton exchange between pyridine and p-toluenesulfonic acid. 2-Chloropyridine, a toxic and environmentally significant breakdown product of the pesticide imidacloprid.
